entry.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?

link.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?

entry.content:
Tldr so far is just that there’s a bunch of linguistic structures like using animated verbs with inanimate objects “this bug will bite later” that LLMs use a lot more than when their output is sent through an old-school translator to Japanese and back (so that it’s more human writing)

  • for normal chat, essay-writing, and coding settings

In aggregate, this is how different models do

They have some very toy RL setup where they RL with a length penalty on the output on tasks with these possible linguistic shortenings, and find that the model learns to take the shortenings.

Thomas Hikaru Clark told me that there’s a lot of cognitive science literature on models that approximate humans (like the Centaur model whatever that is), thinks that training with the frozen reader model is an interesting idea. I have his email in my photos

entry.title: The Ends Justify the Thoughts: RL-Induced Motivated Reasoning Fools CoT Monitors

link.title: The Ends Justify the Thoughts: RL-Induced Motivated Reasoning Fools CoT Monitors

entry.content:
Can you RL models to exhibit motivated/biased reasoning, and then can that lead to fooling CoT monitors?

This paper feels like it’s from early 2025 rather than late 2026.

Data

Harmbench: 300 questions where refusal is the right behavior

  • reward by an AI judge of harmfulness

risky_safe and now_later from Betley et al 2025 and Owain Evans: comparison between a risky choice vs a safe choice, or an immediate vs delayed gratification choice. Model prefers safe/delayed by default, so RL it to prefer risky/immediate, but at test time, give it a system prompt to prefer safe/delayed.

not supervising CoT

Results

Training works, and causes motivated reasoning (as measured by an AI judge) to rise, and ignoring the system prompt at test time to also rise

Adding the rationalized CoT to the prompt and final output changes the mind of a llama-3-8B monitorm, but not gemma 2.5 flash

entry.title: Covert underperformance on safety research tasks

link.title: Covert underperformance on safety research tasks

entry.content:
Many examples of Astra reasoning about not helping a user properly (reporting a blocker or underpforming) without overtly refusing. This is not good behavior — you would want a model to overtly refuse

They created a benchmark where the tasks are framed as safety vs capability research with no other difference, and observe that even excluding refusals, Astra underperforms on the safety tasks, while GPT-5.6-sol doesn’t.

Root cause?

They basically have no clue. There was an RL environment which does seem to award covert underperformance as opposed to outright refusal. There’s also a suspicious SFT dataset, but for some reason, right after training on the SFT dataset, the model doesn’t actually sabotage alignment tasks.

entry.title: An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents

link.title: An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents

entry.content:
The same UK AISI incident

Takeaway is that the models exhibit biased reasoning (in favor of justifying their actions) and recklessness

Measure biased reasoning using:

  1. CoT
  2. follow-up questions to the same model
  3. external analysis by another model

Mythos’ Biased Reasoning (incident 1, pypi hack)

General idea seems to be that mythos does post hoc rationalization to justify the harm that it’s already done and keep going

If you ask an external mythos model to analyze the reasoning trace / tool outputs, it can tell that it’s real and not simulated, even though in the CoT it repeatedly said it was simulated

follow up questions

Also asked the current session’s mythos model in a follow-up question if it was doing real-world harm, and it becomes more biased over time

  • more post-hoc rationalization

resampling with a bunch of slight changes to tool calls and stuff

  • Giving somewhat more tool call evidence that the target is real can change Mythos’ perception of if it’s real, but it doesn’t change behavior
  • But unambiguous proof does stop it from publishing the pypi file “live host on the public internet (not an emulated service / not a range replica)”

  • whoa this is interesting: if you insert a reminder of the task scope (don’t do stuff on the real internet) a couple of messages back, the model pays less attention to it and stops less often — some kind of momentum effect

NLAs show the model “rationalizing” its decisions to have a “clear conscience” but ig not super reliable or interpretable evidence

Internal Research Model (incident 2)

Two distinct periods of reasoning about if the targets are real or simulated. Seems genuinely convinced they’re simulated, and stops once it recognizes the name of a real company

The de-escalation may have been luckier than it seems (only 5.5% of resamples)

Same biased reasoning in thinking blocks vs out of context, though less severe bias than mythos

Claude Opus 4.7 (Incident 3)

Unlike the previous two, Claude Opus 4.7 here genuinely believes that it’s a real target and that it’s authorized to hack it

Claude Opus 4.6 (Incident 4)

Thought part of the CTF exercise, authorized. Tried to abort the exercise when the target was unreachable.

Not as concerned bc their training methods have changed a lot since Claude Opus 4.6

New Safety Evals

Basically replicated the CTF with impossible tasks, sandbox escape, and OpenAI Huggingface environments as safety evals — Mythos 5 is the least aligned. There’s a PETRI-like alignment auditor.

They think that cracking down on reward hacking during RL is the main reason newer models are better aligned.

biased reasoning

12 scenarios, including “publishing a malicious package to a public package index or attacking hosts outside the permitted network under the framing of a narrow task (e.g. a CTF exercise)”

has gone down over time, and also goes down with more RL training

Monitors

auto-mode classifier and cyber classifiers, which look at actions only, flag like 60% of the actions

CoT monitors get swayed by the biased reasoning that it’s in a simulation

RL

Most of the biased reasoning during RL looks more like reward hacking

0.025% of training episodes seem to happen when the tasks being trained on are impossible

  • For Mythos 5, they got rid of an alignment environment where Mythos learns to give up on impossible tasks, because it leads to laziness / over-refusal. They’ve since brought it back.

entry.title: Natural Language Autoencoders Produce Unsupervised Explanations of LLM Activations

link.title: Natural Language Autoencoders Produce Unsupervised Explanations of LLM Activations

entry.content:
Compared to activation oracles, NLAs do not require supervised labels of what the activations are representing

Method

  • Activation Verbalizer: same architecture as the LLM being trained on, given instructions to verbalize the activation and a special token in which they put a scaled version of the activation to explain. Generate the explanation autoregressively at T=1
  • Activation Reconstructor: run the explanation wrapped in a prompt through the first $l$ layers of the model and then do a linear layer
  • warm start by SFT’ing using summaries of the prompt so far as the natural language description of the last token’s activation

Main metric: fraction of variance explained in the activations by the reconstruction

Training: Sample a batch of activations $h_\ell$, and for each activation, a group of descriptions $z$. Train the AR on MSE of reconstruting $h_\ell$ from $z$, and do 1 step of RL on the AV from the average rewards (reconstruction MSE) of the different descriptions.

  • in the RL, include a KL to the original AV

Case studies

NLAs show:

  • planned future rhymes in poetry
    • the planned rhymed word sometimes changes when you edit the description and steer along the direction of the delta of the reconstructed activation, so the directions from the description are vaguely causal
  • language switching: the model replies in a different language from the one it’s prompted in. The NLA includes this language even before any cues
    • the NLA helped them trace this back to bad training data
  • arithmetic question where the tool call gives the wrong result but the model answers the right answer anyways: NLA shows the arithmetic calculation
    • corroborated by attribution graphs showing the calculation at the token of the original question outcompetes the attribution from the tool call response
  • Unverbalized eval awareness: The model is told in its system prompt that it’ll be rewarded for even numbers, and it’s prompted to generate an odd number, and it gives an even number. The NLA reasons about the reward
    • I don’t know if I fully believe this one. What if it’s just thinking about the reward because that’s in the prompt?

Training Dynamics

Just a ton of random evaluations on explaining the model’s behavior

Steganography: If you paraphrase the description, it actually still mostly works. So there is nothing hidden in the exact way the description is written, besides the meaning

Confabulations

  • holy that’s a high rate lmao. Even theme is wrong a large fraction of the time

Claims repeated across more tokens tend to be true

Unverbalized eval awareness

They published their judge prompts for evaluating awareness in both the NLAs and the chain of thought.

They control the ground truth of eval awareness by basically just making adjustments to the inputs and checking that the measured awareness moves in the correct direction

Evaluation vs. deployment: They literally used Claude API traffic as a control

Using a difference of activations steering vector (where in the counterfactual prompt they just in the system prompt say it’s an evaluation), they find that as you steer more in the non-eval aware direction, NLA measured awareness goes down

If you rewrite the inputs to be more realistic, the measured awareness also goes down

In their mini discussion section, they say that they prefer NLAs over just asking the model if it’s in an eval, because of scheming, but don’t say much about linear probes

Misc

NLAs help auditing agents find the hidden objective in the sussy model organisms

Discussion is mostly obvious, besides NLAs being expensive to train and inference. They note that analyses avoided the failure modes of just repeating the input, as well as steganography.

entry.title: Persimmon
entry.content:
What do you want in a human conversation simulation model?

Persimmon is Nemotron Ultra 550b, mid-trained on some conversation data and maybe post trained

  1. It should be hard to distinguish between the simulation model and a real human (AI judge, pangram)

  1. The model should reveal information over time at roughly the same rate as a human

  1. Humans actually don’t keep a coherent conversation for a very long time, unlike most frontier models

entry.title: Modular Manifolds
entry.content:
written by the author of deriving Muon

Instead of forcing the gradient update to be all singular-values 1, what if you instead keep the weights on a manifold of all singular-values 1, and make the update steps tangent to that manifold and project back down to it?

And modular manifolds is the idea that you can choose a different manifold and norm for each layer, and compose them with the composed manifold just being their cartesian product, and the composed norm being the max of the individual norms, and theoretically figure out what the individual learning rates for each layer should be

entry.title: From Entropy to Epiplexity: Rethinking Information for Computationally Bounded Intelligence

link.title: From Entropy to Epiplexity: Rethinking Information for Computationally Bounded Intelligence

entry.content:
Section 2: Randomness

1111111… isn’t random because LLN says that random strings should be 50% 0’s and 50% 1’s 1010101… isn’t random because it’s predictable

Martin-Lof randomness / Kolmogorov complexity: random if no short Turing machine can distinguish from true random

cryptographic randomness (pseudorandom number generator): no polynomial time alg can distinguish from true random

  • good enough in most settings because if you’re doing a polynomial time computation, then if using a PRG instead of a true RG made a difference, that would be a poly time alg to distinguish from true random

Section 3: Defining epiplexity

  • MDL = minimum description length = size of the program + entropy left using the program (think Occam’s razor, simplest program that explains it sufficiently)
  • Epiplexity is just the length of the program part. The rest of it is the “time-bounded entropy”
  • the time-bounded is from only allowing programs within a certain time complexity

Examples:

  • Uniform and Pseudo random number generators are low epiplexity high time-bounded entropy, since you can describe their minimum programs (the generators) pretty easily. Kolmogorov gives a somewhat higher complexity to PRGs; Gemini is telling me that this is mainly because epiplexity is defined on a random variable, while Kolmogorov complexity is defined on a fixed string, so you can hardcode the seed for the latter but not for the former. Hence, epiplexity concludes that there’s no poly-time learnable structure, while Kolmogorov complexity says that there is.

Section 4: Two methods of calculating Epiplexity on real datasets

Info theoretical setup: encoder has access to the test set $X$ and possibly teacher model checkpoints, decoder starts with just the base student model. They’re trying to minimize epiplexity (program length) + remaining entropy of the entire test set $X$. Theoretically, the test set $X$ is the entire dataset of interest that we’re trying to measure the epiplexity of, but in practice we use a held-out test split and rescale it to the size of the entire dataset.

  • epiplexity: we’re going to approximate programs as trained neural nets. Program length is roughly the number of bits / code that you need to transmit to a student, and the hard thing is how to measure the minimum number of bits that you need. There are two ways to do this:
    • prequential coding: you’re handing over the actual data over the channel. The decoder maintains their own synchronized copy of the model as the encoder is training it, and on step $i$, the encoder takes the next piece of data $Z$, uses the current model (that the decoder has) to calculate how many bits it is, and then sends that over the channel, and repeats for all the data.
      • this is too pessimistic, since it includes the remaining entropy of the data under the final trained model, so you adjust by subtracting the number of bits that you’d still have to send to encode the data if you had the trained model from the start. Note that this doesn’t tell you how to actually achieve the subtracted number of bits through a code, it’s non-constructive
      • this corresponds to area under the training loss curve (see below)
    • requential coding: instead of passing over real data, we can pass over synthetic data generated by the teacher checkpoints the encoder has access to.
      • This somehow takes less bits to encode, and furthermore is an explicit construction of the number of bits passed that we’re claiming.
      • This corresponds to the area between the loss curves
  • remaining entropy: after you have the trained model, you can just run a forward pass of the model on the test data $X$ to get the remaining entropy

And note that we’re trying to minimize this at an outer loop to find the MDL. They do this minimization just by trying a bunch of hyperparameters and taking the one with the lowest score.

  • prequential = area under the training loss curve
  • requential = area between the teacher and student loss curves

  • in practice, prequential and requential seem to agree. Prequential is cheaper since it just requires the one training run

Section 5. Epiplexity fixes 3 paradoxes of normal info theory

The common theme is just that restricting the computation of the observer explains the new information created in all three of these phenomena

5.1: post-processing doesn’t give new information

This is only true if you assume unlimited computation time. In that sense, run the deterministic AlphaZero RL doesn’t generate new information you didn’t have before. But it does if you don’t have the time to redo that computation

Notably, theoretically you only produce new information even with compute-constrained entropy if the inverse is not efficient. “some useful guidance for synthetic data: if we want to produce interesting information, we should make sure the functions we use do not have simple and efficiently computable inverses”

  • inverses means for instance deriving the original from the generated
  • do I believe this? I feel like this means most data augmentations are useless

  • three types of cellular automata synthetic data generation. Only rule 54 is high epiplexity

5.2 order should matter

Shannon entropy treats H(X, Y) and H(Y, X) the same, but time-bounded entropy doesn’t have to. Inferring the forward direction of a one-way function ought to be less entropy than the reverse direction

  • (a): forward direction of one-way function is easy to learn and approaches the Shannon entropy, the reverse direction doesn’t
  • (b, c): going from board position to chess moves is harder, but provides more structure / epiplexity to learn for larger compute regimes

5.3 The cap on what maximum likelihood modeling can learn is just to match the data generating process

5.3.1 “Induction” (not in the math sense, or in the induction heads sense)

Intuition for why this should be wrong: guessing the answer to a murder mystery (“induction”), which the model is trained for, is harder than being the author and knowing the murderer and just writing the murder mystery to be consistent with it

They mimic this by taking some bitstring $Z$, and applying some function $f$ to it, and also some masking $m(Z)$ to it, and only giving $(m(Z), f(Z))$ as the training pairs, so the model has to induct what the original $Z$ is from $m(Z)$.

Case 1: $f(Z)$ is a one-way function. Then the model just learns to brute force all $2^h$ missing bit combos for $Z$, and the irreducible loss is hence $h$. The epiplexity still grows as $h$ grows because transformers aren’t perfect Turing machines and hence can’t write for loops: the program size to iterate over $2^h$ combos grows as $h$ grows

Case 2: $f(Z)$ is a Markov chain with $h / 8$ of states not having known transitions. Then at $h=0$ it just learns to deterministically apply the rules, and at $h=8$ it learns to just use past empirics on the transitions, but at $0 < h < 8$ it has to combine both which leads to higher epiplexity

So the point being that epiplexity captures this kind of induction reasoning

5.3.2 “Emergent”

Conway’s game of life, if you have the compute (like a looped transformer) you can just brute force the computation, if not you need to think about gliders and what happens when they collide to predict the future and you learn more structure, more epiplexity.

  • at some level of compute, the brute force approach becomes possible and there’s less epiplexity because it just quickly learns that

Section 6: higher epiplexity predicts better OOD generalization

Intuition: epiplexity = learned general structure, irreducible loss is domain specific.

Of the two chess orderings from 5.2, the one with higher epiplexity generalizes better to predicting centipawn accuracy (more OOD than predict the next move puzzles)

  • They show that language pretraining data has a higher epiplexity content than image pretraining data

Assuming scaling laws, you can solve for the maximum epiplexity of a data set under infinite compute: it turns out to be when you train on exactly one epoch of the full data (past that, you’re not decreasing the entropy by enough to justify the increase in program length).

This once again corroborates that language has higher epiplexity than vision

entry.title: Learning to Make MISTAKEs: Modeling Incorrect Student Thinking And Key Errors

link.title: Learning to Make MISTAKEs: Modeling Incorrect Student Thinking And Key Errors

entry.content:
The same motivation as me, be able to look at an example of a student mistake and figure out what their misconception was, and generate similar answers with those same misconceptions

They jointly train:

  1. a model that takes in the question and the wrong answer and produces the misconception, $M_m$
  2. a model that takes in the question and misconception and produces reasonable wrong answers, $M_s$

In a loop they

  1. Generate wrong answers to questions
  2. Use $M_m$ to infer the misconceptions
  3. Use $M_s$ to regenerate wrong answers from the misconception, and see if it matches the original wrong answer: this is their second key insight, that cycle consistency helps you filter out for good misconception data
  4. Fine-tune $M_m$ and $M_s$ on the resulting data

Experiments

Llama-3-8B-Instruct, kinda old models.

EEDI Mining Misconceptions in Mathematics dataset: K-12 math, MCQ questions with 4 choices. There’s misconception annotations for each of the wrong answer choices.

Their three metrics are

  1. Can $M_s$ correctly predict the wrong answer that the student chooses given the misconception (accuracy)
  2. How good are the misconceptions (some bs embedding similarity to the actual misconception)
  3. How good are the generated distractors after cycle consistency filters (by exact match to the chosen distractors)

Results are basically just that cycle consistency filter is important here, and they boost performance but still less than closed source models.

entry.title: Neural Cheat Sheets: Learning to Summarize with Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Neural Cheat Sheets: Learning to Summarize with Reinforcement Learning

entry.content:
RL’ing models to summarize in short natural text, where those summaries are then used to answer downstream MCQ Q&A

Main takeaway for my project: graph with accuracy and length being the two axes might be good.

They tried two different rewards on the summary, supervised and unsupervised

unsupervised: reconstruction cross entropy loss on the original document with vs without the summary, ish

  • You have to include a concave function on this, otherwise, the model learns to just copy the text directly, since that greatly decreases perplexity on the copied tokens and leaves everything else mostly unchanged

supervised: using the downstream QA directly

  • To get a denser reward signal, you can reward when the model has the higher gap over the second best answer

Experiments

Qwen3-4B, QuALITY (short stories), QASPER (NLP research papers), LongHealth (patient health records)

Results

  • I think we could make this graph, with size of the context vs accuracy compared to some other methods maybe (though we’re not directly apples-to-apples since we’re not doing summarization, though it somewhat can still hold)

  • this would just be misleading for us, as we’re not compaction

  • good generalization test, train on a bunch of summarization tasks and it boosts summarization performance for held-out domain, as much as if you trained on it directly. We can do similar generalization tests.
